source.title: Generalization in Kernel Regression Under Realistic Assumptions

record.tranche_reason: The study reports kernel-regression variance curves described as multiple descent, using kernel simulations rather than the original deep-network model-size sweep. It does not test most of the listed versions.
record.gate_note: Figure 1 reports multiple-descent variance curves for two kernels and explicitly describes the phenomenon. Figure 2 reports apparently diverging variance for a Gaussian process kernel in a low-dimensional setting. Theorems 3 and 4 give bounds on excess risk for interpolating kernel regression, but do not sweep model size, epochs, or sample size to test a double-descent curve. Results cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: Mostly a theory paper on excess-risk bounds for kernel regression. Its Figure 1 simulations show noise-only (variance) error of unregularized kernel regression with several descents, in a polynomial kernel and a 3-layer NTK. The authors tie this to the multiple-descent shape implied by Theorem 3. That is a new setting (min-norm kernel regression on the sphere) bearing on the multiple-peak, noise-driven part of V6. The original deep-network size, epoch and sample sweeps are not reproduced.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors give bounds for kernel regression under realistic assumptions, valid for any regularization, noise, dimension and sample size. They attribute good generalization to kernel self-regularization: benign overfitting in high dimensions, nearly tempered overfitting in fixed dimensions. They also note their Theorem 3 rates reflect the known multiple descent of kernel ridge(less) regression.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes kernel regression theoretically and includes kernel variance simulations; it does not reproduce the original deep-network size, epoch, or sample-size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported overfitting behavior and bounds depend on input dimension, kernel spectrum and type, target-function spectrum, noise, and regularization.

fits_no_version.finding: A low-dimensional 3-layer GPK shows apparently diverging median variance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In low dimensions, unregularized kernel-regression variance for common kernels can grow with n rather than staying O(1).

fits_no_version.finding: Interpolating kernel regression is benign in high dimensions (Thm 3) and nearly tempered in fixed dimension (Thm 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether interpolation generalizes benignly or temperedly depends on the dimension regime, kernel spectrum and target.

record.problems: The plotted variance values are not stated numerically in the text. The multiple-descent evidence is limited to two kernel simulations; the paper does not empirically sweep model size, epochs, or sample size, and does not test whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peaks.
record.rows_left_out: No other result directly tests the listed double-descent versions. Theorems 1, 2, and 5 provide eigenvalue or risk bounds, but do not report a double-descent curve or test a listed claim version.

untested.parts: Whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peaks; triple descent as such; label noise versus a clean-label control.
No explicit statement that adding samples raises test error near a threshold, though the Figure 1 axis may be sample count.
Effective ranks are used in the bounds but are not tested as predictors of peak location.
No re-plotting against an effective parameter count.

missing.what: The x-axis of Figure 1 (likely n or τ = log n / log d, with one curve per d) is needed to tell whether the descents run along the sample axis, which bears on V3.
missing.locator: Figure 1 and Section 5.1 discussion after Theorem 3

record.verdict_notes: The multiple-descent evidence is a side illustration in a theory paper; the phenomenon is attributed to Liang & Rakhlin (2020) and Xiao & Pennington (2022). The only measured quantity is variance, which isolates the noise-driven component. No regularized curves are plotted. Theorem 5 covers regularized rates but not removal of the peaks. Tranche set to T3 rather than the record's T2, because the setting is kernel regression on the sphere rather than a different method on deep networks.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep or test-error curve around an interpolation threshold.
No sample-size comparison near an interpolation threshold showing that more samples raise test error.
No capacity sweep across model classes showing risk improves again after interpolation.
The study defines effective-rank and concentration quantities for its bounds, but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across axes.

Figure 1 reports multiple descent in unregularized kernel-regression variance. It does not isolate label noise as the cause, test whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peaks, or establish triple descent.
No comparison of descent curves against an effective parameter count.

rows.operation_detail: Varied input dimension and measured variance of unregularized kernel regression.
rows.measure: Variance of unregularized kernel regression, measured by MSE.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence region over 50 trials with 2500 test samples each
rows.note: The text describes multiple descent and says it becomes more pronounced as input dimension grows; it also says the MSE at the valleys decreases.
rows.check: The operation is likely mis-described. The caption says multiple descent grows 'as the input dimension grows', which suggests curves for several d plotted against another axis, probably sample count (n ~ d^τ per Theorem 3). The text never states the x-axis, so 'varied input dimension' as the swept variable is unverified.

rows.subject: GPK corresponding to a 3-layer fully-connected network
rows.operation_detail: Measured variance of unregularized kernel regression in a low-dimensional setting.

conditions.value: uniformly on the unit disk {x ∈ R² : ‖x‖ ≤ 1}

rows.measure: Variance; the figure caption calls the plotted summary the median variance.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence region over 100 trials with 5000 test samples each
rows.note: The text characterizes the variance as apparently diverging in low dimensions and says the example suggests some previous upper bounds may be overly optimistic. The plotted values are not given in the text.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked: this is a low-dimensional variance-divergence example, not a descent curve.

rows.subject: Dot-product kernel satisfying Theorem 3 assumptions (including NTK, Laplace, or RBF)
rows.operation_detail: Derived a high-dimensional excess-risk bound for the min-norm interpolating solution.

conditions.value: n, d → ∞ with d/nᵗᵃᵘ = Θₙ,ᵈ(1), τ ∈ (0, ∞) \ N

rows.measure: Upper bounds on excess-risk variance and bias.
rows.value: V ≤ σ²ε · Oₙ,ᵈ(1/d^(τ−⌊τ⌋) + 1/d^(⌊τ⌋+1−τ)); bias bounded in terms of target-function projections as stated in Theorem 3.
rows.note: This establishes benign overfitting for specified interpolating kernel-regression settings, but does not report a capacity sweep or a double-descent curve.
rows.check: The Theorem 3 variance bound decays slowest when τ is near an integer. The authors say this 'highlights the multiple descent behavior', so the row bears on V6. As an upper bound, it cannot by itself show that peaks occur.

source_check.correct: The scaling assumption is d^τ/n = Θ_{n,d}(1), equivalently n = Θ_{n,d}(d^τ), with τ ∈ (0,∞) excluding integers; it is not d/n^τ = Θ_{n,d}(1). The stated variance upper bound agrees with Theorem 3.
source_check.locator_found: Theorem 3, Section 5.1, lines 769–847; Appendix E.3, lines 4470–4484; Section 2.2, line 266.
source_check.problem: The dimension/sample-size scaling ratio is transcribed incorrectly.

rows.subject: Kernel with polynomially decaying eigenvalues λᵢ = Θᵢ,ₙ(i⁻¹⁻ᵃ)
rows.operation_detail: Derived an excess-risk bound for the min-norm interpolating solution in fixed dimension.
rows.measure: Upper bounds on excess-risk variance and bias.
rows.value: V ≤ σ²ε Õₙ(n²ᵃ); if θᵢ* = Oᵢ(i⁻ʳ) and r > a, B ≤ Õₙ(1/n^min(2(r−a), 2−a)).
rows.note: The authors call this nearly tempered overfitting; it is a bound for interpolation, not a measured double-descent curve.
rows.check: A fixed-dimension interpolation bound with no descent curve; correctly unlinked.

source_check.correct: V ≤ σ²_ε Õ_n(n^{2a}); B ≤ (1/δ) Õ_n(n^{-min(2(r−a),2−a)}), with probability at least 1−δ−O_n(1/log n).
source_check.locator_found: Theorem 4, Section 5.2, lines 976–992; repeated in Appendix E.2, lines 4205–4228.
source_check.problem: The bias bound omits the theorem's explicit 1/δ factor.
